V1.1.1.note: Fastify decodes the URL and parses JSON once, before the schema runs; nothing is decoded after validation.

V1.1.2.note: Output is encoded by the thing that emits it: Fastify's JSON serialiser for the API, React for the website, and the JSON-LD writer escapes "<" (F165).

V1.2.1.note: Website HTML is rendered by React, which escapes text and attributes; the one raw insertion (JSON-LD) escapes "<".

V1.2.2.note: Request-derived URL parts are encoded (the sign-in token, the RevenueCat account id, which can only be one path segment); catalogue links are https only.

V1.2.3.note: JSON is produced by serialisers, never by string building; the website's JSON-LD escapes "<" so a value cannot end its script tag.

V1.2.4.note: Every SQL statement is parameterised or fixed text, exercised against real Postgres.

V1.2.5.note: No operating-system commands: the API and website run none (no child_process anywhere in their code).

V1.2.9.note: No regular expression is built from user input; the few built at run time are assembled from constants.

V1.3.2.note: No eval() or new Function in the code; CodeQL scans every push for code injection.

V1.3.3.note: Data bound for a risky context is neutralised there: CSV exports prefix formula characters, the coach fences user data and strips its fence tags, crash reports are scrubbed.

V1.3.4.note: No user-supplied SVG is accepted or shown.

V1.3.5.note: No user-supplied Markdown, CSS or templates are rendered (the blog's text is ours, in code).

V1.3.6.note: Every outbound call is inventoried and goes only to its fixed host; a new call site fails the test until reviewed.

V1.3.7.note: No template is built from user input: the sign-in email is fixed plain text holding only the link and code the server made.

V1.3.9.note: The only cache server (Redis, optional) holds rate-limit counters keyed by IP address or account id, which a client cannot shape into commands.

V1.3.10.note: No format-string functions take untrusted input (logs are structured objects).

V1.3.11.note: Email goes through Resend's HTTP API as JSON, never raw SMTP; the address is schema-validated, the subject fixed.

V1.4.1.note: A memory-managed runtime (Node.js) with no native code of our own.

V1.4.2.note: Numbers are bounded where they arrive: spend 0 to 100 million, vector-clock counts 0 to 2^40, parsed amounts at most $10 million, whole numbers only.

V1.4.3.note: A memory-managed runtime (Node.js) with no native code of our own.

V1.5.1.note: No XML is parsed anywhere (the RSS feed is written, never read).

V1.5.2.note: Only JSON is deserialised, into plain objects checked by schemas; prototype-pollution keys are refused at the parser.

V2.1.1.note: Every data item's rule is documented, from the schemas.

V2.1.2.note: Rules for data that must agree with other data are documented.

V2.1.3.note: Per-user and global limits are documented with the test that holds each.

V2.2.1.note: Every input route parses its schema first; values each rule allows and just outside it are sent to every route.

V2.2.2.note: Validation happens in the API; the app's own checks are for usability only.

V2.2.3.note: Combined data is checked: a household write comes from a member and lands on their own line; a refresh token must be live and unrotated; a provider token's nonce must match.

V2.3.1.note: Steps can't be skipped: a session needs a link or code issued for that address, or a provider token with this sign-in's nonce.

V2.3.2.note: The documented limits are enforced and tested.

V2.3.3.note: Operations that touch storage succeed whole or are put back: a sync change or household change the database refuses is undone in memory, and account deletion says "deleted" only once every part is durable (F75).

V2.3.4.note: Capped resources (households per owner, members per household) are checked and changed in one synchronous step in a single process; running one instance is required and warned about at boot.

V2.4.1.note: Every route has a rate limit; costly ones are tighter (the AI coach: 10 per account per minute; sign-in: 5 or 10 per IP).

V3.2.1.note: API answers are JSON with nosniff and a deny-all framing policy; the website serves its own pages only.

V3.2.2.note: Text is rendered by React as text; the only raw HTML is the escaped JSON-LD and a fixed theme script, allowed by CSP hash.

V3.3.1.note: No cookies: neither the website nor the API sets one (the theme choice is in localStorage; the API authenticates with bearer tokens).

V3.3.2.note: No cookies: neither the website nor the API sets one (the theme choice is in localStorage; the API authenticates with bearer tokens).

V3.4.1.note: HSTS on every response: the website two years with subdomains and preload; the API one year with subdomains.

V3.4.2.note: CORS answers only exact origins from the allowlist; a look-alike or a wildcard allows nothing.

V3.4.3.note: CSP on every response: the website with object-src 'none', base-uri 'self' and per-page script hashes (no unsafe-inline scripts); the API with frame-ancestors 'none'.

V3.4.4.note: nosniff on every response of the website and the API.

V3.4.5.note: The website sends strict-origin-when-cross-origin; the API no-referrer.

V3.4.6.note: frame-ancestors 'none' on the website and the API.

V3.5.1.note: No cookie-based authentication: a request is authorised only by an Authorization header, which another site's page cannot add without a CORS preflight the API refuses.

V3.5.2.note: Sensitive routes need the Authorization header, which forces a preflight; a request that avoids the preflight carries no token and gets 401.

V3.5.3.note: State changes use POST or DELETE, except GET /auth/verify, which uses up a sign-in link (the app opens it from the email). No cookies are involved, so another site can't ride it, but it is a GET that changes state.

V3.5.4.note: The website (zenoapp.in, Netlify) and the API (Render) are separate hosts.

V3.5.5.note: No postMessage listeners in the website.

V3.7.1.note: Only current web technology (React and Next.js); no plugins.

V3.7.2.note: The only automatic redirect is www to the apex domain, our own; links to other sites are links the user follows.

V4.1.1.note: API answers declare application/json; charset=utf-8, errors included; the RSS feed declares utf-8.

V4.1.2.note: The website redirects http to https as it should. The API also answers http with a 301 to https: Render does this for every service and it cannot be switched off there. The app only ever uses the https address.

V4.1.3.note: Client-written X-Forwarded-For entries are ignored; only the hops the load balancer adds are trusted (whole numbers only).

V4.2.1.note: A request with both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding is refused with 400 on a real socket, and a smuggled second request is never answered. (Render's load balancer in front is not tested here.)

V6.3.1.note: As documented: per-IP limits, 5 emails per address per 15 minutes, 10 wrong codes per address per 24 hours.

V6.3.2.note: No default accounts exist. The demo sign-in is refused in production whatever is configured.

V6.3.3.note: Every pathway is a single factor (an inbox, or an Apple or Google account). The rationale (the money data lives on the phone behind its own PIN lock; the server holds account, household and billing state) is documented; adding a second factor is a product decision.

V6.3.4.note: Every route is classified, and a new one fails the matrix until it is; every pathway is documented, with the same session at the end.

V6.4.1.note: Sign-in links (256 random bits) and codes (6 digits from a CSPRNG) expire after 10 minutes and work once; they never become a long-term credential.

V6.4.2.note: No password hints or security questions exist anywhere in the sign-in code.

V6.4.3.note: No passwords to reset: a lost session is replaced by a new sign-in link.

V6.4.4.note: No multi-factor authentication factors to lose.

V6.5.1.note: A sign-in link and a code each work once.

V6.5.2.note: No lookup secrets (backup codes) exist. (Sign-in link tokens are stored only as a hash.)

V6.5.3.note: Codes come from crypto.randomInt, link tokens from crypto.randomBytes(32).

V6.5.4.note: Codes are 6 random digits (about 20 bits), links 256 bits.

V6.6.1.note: No SMS or phone delivery of codes.

V6.6.2.note: A code is replaced by the next one requested, and on the phone a link works only for a request made there for the same email. Gap: an earlier LINK stays usable for the rest of its 10 minutes after a newer one is requested.

V6.6.3.note: Codes: 10 verifications per IP per minute and 10 wrong codes per address per 24 hours. Links carry 256 bits.

V6.8.1.note: Accounts are namespaced by provider (acct_apple_ and acct_google_ plus the provider's user id); a provider's email never selects an account.

V6.8.2.note: Apple and Google tokens are refused unsigned (alg none), with another algorithm, signed by another key, or tampered with.

V6.8.4.note: No function requires a stronger or more recent sign-in; the documented assumption is single-factor strength for every pathway.

V7.1.1.note: Inactivity (30 days) and the absence of an absolute lifetime are documented, the latter as an owner decision (V7.3.2).

V7.1.2.note: Documented: sessions per account are not capped; each device sign-in is its own session.

V7.1.3.note: Documented: a session started with Apple or Google is independent of the provider's own session.

V7.2.1.note: Every token is verified by the API (one guard for all protected routes); the app never decides for itself.

V7.2.2.note: Sessions are per-sign-in tokens (RS256 access JWTs, random refresh tokens), never static keys.

V7.2.3.note: Refresh tokens are 256 bits from crypto.randomBytes, stored only as a hash.

V7.2.4.note: Each sign-in issues a new session. Gap: signing in again does not end the device's previous session on the server; it lasts until its refresh token expires or is used.

V7.3.1.note: A session unused for 30 days ends: its refresh token is refused at 30 days and works the second before.

V7.3.2.note: No absolute lifetime: each refresh starts a new 30 days, so an app in use stays signed in. Documented; whether to cap it (signing users out periodically) is a product decision.

V7.4.1.note: Sign-out revokes the refresh token at once. Gap (F77): the access token works until it expires, at most 15 minutes; a per-account revocation time already exists for account deletion.

V7.4.2.note: Deleting an account ends every session, link and code of that account, then every access token issued before it.

V7.4.3.note: No authentication factor can be changed (no passwords, no MFA settings).

V7.4.4.note: The only authenticated surface is the app; sign-out is on its Profile screen.

V7.4.5.note: There are no administrators and no operator tool to end a user's sessions short of deleting the account.

V7.5.1.note: No account attribute used for sign-in can be changed: there is no email change, phone number or MFA setting.

V7.5.2.note: Users cannot list or end their other sessions.

V7.6.1.note: Documented: a Zeno session neither follows nor ends the Apple or Google session.

V7.6.2.note: A session starts only after the user chooses a pathway and confirms it (opens the link, enters the code, or approves with Apple or Google); the app also requires the age consent first.

V8.1.1.note: Function-level (public, own secret, signed in) and data-level rules (own data only; households for members) are documented.

V8.1.2.note: Field-level rule documented: a member changes only their own spend line; there are no other roles.

V8.2.1.note: Every route's access is pinned; a new route fails the matrix until it is classified.

V8.2.2.note: The account comes from the verified token, never a parameter; a stranger gets 403 on a household with identical bodies, an unknown id 404.

V8.2.3.note: A member's spend write lands on their own line whatever the body says; the member id comes from the token.

V8.3.1.note: Every decision is made in the API; the app holds no authority.

V8.4.1.note: Households are the only shared space; every household route checks membership first.

V9.1.1.note: Signatures are checked before claims are used, for our tokens and the providers'.

V9.1.2.note: RS256 only: alg none, HS256 and a missing key id are refused.

V9.1.3.note: Keys come only from our own configured key pair and from Apple's and Google's fixed JWKS URLs, chosen by kid; jku, x5u and jwk headers are never read.

V9.2.1.note: exp to the second, and nbf when present, for our tokens and the providers'.

V9.2.2.note: Access tokens need our issuer and audience, which provider ID tokens never carry; refresh tokens are opaque and only accepted by /auth/refresh.

V9.2.3.note: Our audience is checked on every access token; a provider token must carry our client id.

V9.2.4.note: Our signing key issues tokens for one audience only (zeno-mobile).

V10.1.1.note: Tokens live only in the app's keychain and travel only to our API (and Gmail's to Google); the website handles none.

V10.1.2.note: Each sign-in has its own random nonce; the provider gets its SHA-256, the API checks the token carries it (F10).

V10.2.1.note: Gmail connect uses the code flow with PKCE (a code_verifier, no client secret).

V10.2.2.note: Each provider's tokens are checked against that provider's own issuer, keys and audience: an Apple token is refused on the Google route and the reverse.

V10.3.1.note: The API accepts only access tokens with its audience.

V10.3.2.note: The account (sub) is the basis of every decision; no scope or delegation claims are issued.

V10.3.3.note: Users are identified by sub, an account id derived once and never reassigned, under our single issuer.

V10.3.4.note: No route requires a particular sign-in strength or recency.

V11.1.1.note: Key policy written: for each key, how it is made, stored, used, rotated and destroyed (NIST SP 800-57 lifecycle); each key used for one purpose only.

V11.1.2.note: Inventory of every key, algorithm and certificate, read from the code, with where each key may and may not be used.

V11.2.1.note: Only standard implementations: node:crypto (OpenSSL 3) on the server; react-native-quick-crypto (OpenSSL), expo-crypto and SQLCipher 4.7.0 on the phone. Nothing hand-written.

V11.2.2.note: Formats carry their algorithm or version: RS256 in each token header, a key id in each sealed envelope (with a ring of previous keys), a version and iteration count beside each PIN verifier (already migrated once, v2 to v3). A change is a code release, not a setting.

V11.2.3.note: Everything is at 128 bits or more except the JWT signing key, RSA 2048 (about 112 bits). A 3072-bit pair is generated and waiting to go into Render.

V11.3.1.note: No ECB and no RSA encryption anywhere (so no PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding). RS256 signatures use PKCS#1 v1.5 signature padding, which is what Apple, Google and our tokens use and is approved for signatures (FIPS 186-5).

V11.3.2.note: AES-256-GCM on the server; on the phone SQLCipher's AES-256-CBC with a per-page HMAC-SHA512 (encrypt-then-MAC).

V11.3.3.note: All encrypted data is authenticated: GCM's tag on the server (a modified envelope does not open), SQLCipher's per-page HMAC on the phone.

V11.4.1.note: SHA-256 for hashing and HMAC, SHA-512 inside SQLCipher; no MD5 or SHA-1 anywhere.

V11.4.2.note: No user passwords exist (sign-in is by email link or code, Apple or Google). The one password-like secret, the app-lock PIN, is stored as PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations and a random salt.

V11.4.3.note: SHA-256 (256-bit output) for signatures and token hashes.

V11.4.4.note: Keys from secrets use PBKDF2: the PIN at 600,000 iterations; the phone database key through SQLCipher's PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 at 256,000.

V11.5.1.note: Secrets are from the CSPRNG: sign-in links and refresh tokens 256 bits, the device database key 244. The household share code is about 40 bits, short so people can type it, and guessing is bounded by a rate limit and the 5-member cap. (The 6-digit sign-in code is a one-time code, bounded under V6.)

V11.6.1.note: Keys are generated by OpenSSL (RSA, AES via openssl rand) and the platform CSPRNG on the phone; signatures are RS256 through node:crypto.

V12.1.1.note: Measured 2026-10-05 on the API and the website: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 refused, 1.2 and 1.3 accepted, 1.3 chosen when offered.

V12.1.2.note: Measured 2026-10-05 on both hosts with TLS 1.2: ECDHE with AES-GCM accepted (chosen first); every RSA-key-exchange suite (no forward secrecy) and every CBC suite refused by the server. TLS 1.3 has only AEAD suites. (3DES, RC4 and NULL could not be offered: the local OpenSSL lacks them.)

V12.2.1.note: Every client connection is HTTPS: HSTS on both hosts; the app uses only the https API address. (The API host also answers plain http with a redirect, recorded under V4.1.2.)

V12.2.2.note: Publicly trusted certificates (seen 2026-10-05): Google Trust Services for the API (through Render), Let's Encrypt for zenoapp.in (through Netlify).

V12.3.1.note: Every connection is encrypted: outbound calls are https to fixed hosts; Postgres over TLS (on by default, a typo fails closed to "verify"); no SSH or management channel of ours.

V12.3.2.note: Every TLS client verifies certificates (Node's default) except the Postgres connection: Render's internal database uses a self-signed certificate it does not support verifying. Traffic stays on Render's private network. Accepted in P0.3.

V12.3.3.note: No internal HTTP services: one API process and its database.

V12.3.4.note: The only internal connection, to Postgres, uses Render's self-signed certificate, unverified (see V12.3.2).

V13.1.1.note: Every connection is documented (the data-flow diagram), and every outbound call site is inventoried in a test that fails on a new one. No user can make the server call a URL of their choosing.

V13.2.1.note: Each backend link has its own credential: Postgres (Render-generated), the RevenueCat webhook (a shared secret, compared in constant time), /metrics (its own token), each provider its own key.

V13.2.2.note: The API connects to Postgres as the database owner Render creates; there is no separate role with only the rights it needs.

V13.2.3.note: No default credentials: the database password is generated by Render; secrets are random values the owner made; production refuses to start without its keys.

V13.2.4.note: The allowlist is in code: each outbound call goes to a fixed host, and the inventory test fails on any new call site until reviewed.

V13.2.5.note: The allowlist is enforced by the code only (V13.2.4); Render offers no outbound firewall to enforce it at the network.

V13.3.1.note: Secrets live in Render's environment settings and the owner's offline key folder, never in the repository (gitleaks on every commit and the full history). Render is not a key vault, and keys that were pasted into a chat must be rotated.

V13.3.2.note: Each secret is read only by the process that needs it, and only the owner's Render account can see them; the website build is checked for leaked server secrets.

V13.4.1.note: No source-control metadata is served: /.git/config is 404 on both hosts (measured 2026-10-05); the API serves no files, the website only its build output.

V13.4.2.note: Production runs with NODE_ENV=production: no debug routes, the website a production build, the logger at info, demo sign-in off unless its password is set.

V13.4.3.note: No directory listings: the API serves no files, and Netlify does not list directories.

V13.4.4.note: TRACE is refused on a real socket and never echoes the request.

V13.4.5.note: No API documentation is served; /metrics needs its token in production and fails closed when the token is unset.

V14.1.1.note: Sensitive data identified and put into four protection levels.

V14.1.2.note: Each level has its encryption, integrity, retention, logging and access rules written down.

V14.2.1.note: Sensitive values travel in headers and bodies, except the email sign-in link, which carries a one-time token in its query string (GET /auth/verify). It works once, expires in 10 minutes, and is never logged (F9).

V14.2.2.note: Every API answer says Cache-Control: no-store (F217); there is no cache in front of the API, and Redis (if used) holds only rate-limit counters.

V14.2.3.note: No trackers in the website or the app. Crash reports go to Sentry only when configured, scrubbed of amounts, names, emails and tokens.

V14.2.4.note: The rules of each level are implemented and tested: encryption and integrity (GCM, SQLCipher), retention (account deletion leaves no row), logging (no secret or email in any log line).

V14.3.1.note: Signing out removes the tokens from the keychain; "Erase this device" removes the user's data from the phone. The website holds no authenticated data.

V14.3.2.note: Cache-Control: no-store on every API answer, errors included (F217).

V14.3.3.note: The website's browser storage holds one value, the light or dark theme.

V15.1.1.note: Remediation time frames written: high and critical before the next deploy (CI blocks), exceptions with a reason and an expiry of at most 3 months, moderate and low reviewed in 30 days.

V15.1.2.note: A CycloneDX SBOM of the whole lockfile on every CI run; packages only from the npm registry, pinned by integrity hashes; Actions pinned by commit.

V15.1.3.note: Costly functions listed (the AI coach, sign-in email, provider key fetches, sync) with the limits that protect availability.

V15.2.1.note: As of 2026-10-05: no high or critical advisory outside the expiring allowlist; the 4 moderate ones reviewed and recorded, none reaching the API or website at run time.

V15.2.2.note: Limits implemented and tested: per-route and per-account rate limits, a 30 s deadline on the coach, 8 s on every outbound call, bounded inputs.

V15.2.3.note: No test code or samples ship. But production serves routes the app does not use (/sync, /public-api/keys, /business/summary, the open-banking intents) and a Plaid development adapter.

V15.3.1.note: Handlers build each answer from named fields (for example /account returns only the account id and plan); no stored record is returned whole.

V15.3.2.note: Outbound calls never follow a redirect: refused, and the target never called, on a real socket (F218).

V15.3.3.note: Bodies are parsed by schemas that keep only the declared fields; a household member's write lands on their own line whatever the body says.

V15.3.4.note: The client IP comes from a bounded number of trusted proxy hops; client-written X-Forwarded-For entries are ignored.

V15.3.5.note: TypeScript in strict mode; inputs are parsed by schemas into exact types; the one route reading its query without a schema refuses a repeated parameter instead of coercing it (F219).

V15.3.6.note: Prototype-pollution keys are refused at the JSON parser; schemas produce fresh objects.

V15.3.7.note: Each route reads its parameters from one place (query or body, never merged); a parameter sent twice is refused with 400 (F219).

V16.1.1.note: Logging inventory: each layer, what it logs, the format, where it goes, who can read it, how long it is kept.

V16.2.1.note: Each line has when (UTC time), where (host, route), what (method, path, status) and the client IP and request id, but not the account: who did something is reconstructed from IP and time.

V16.2.2.note: Timestamps are epoch milliseconds (UTC) from the host clock, which Render keeps synchronised.

V16.2.3.note: Logs go only where the inventory says: stdout (Render), the operator's alert webhook for a 5xx, and Sentry on the phone when configured.

V16.2.4.note: JSON lines (pino), readable by any log processor.

V16.2.5.note: No secret, token, query string, body or email address is logged: redaction by path, a request serializer that drops the query, tested with markers.

V16.3.1.note: Every sign-in attempt, success or failure, appears as its request line with route and status, but there is no event naming the account and the method used.

V16.3.2.note: A refused request (401, 403) appears as its request line with route and status, but without the account or the reason.

V16.3.3.note: Attempts to get past validation and rate limits show as 400 and 429 request lines; there is no dedicated security-event log.

V16.3.4.note: Unexpected errors are logged at error level with the request id and sent to the alert webhook; an outside service failing (a provider down, a TLS error reaching it) is logged as a warning with the error.

V16.4.1.note: Every log line is a JSON object written by pino, which escapes control characters, so a value cannot start a new line.

V16.4.2.note: The app only writes to stdout and cannot read or change stored logs. Who can read them is the Render workspace; its members and two-factor sign-in are the owner's to confirm.

V16.4.3.note: Logs are held by Render, outside the application, but there is no separate system for analysis and alerting beyond the 5xx webhook.

V16.5.1.note: Every 4xx and 5xx answer is a fixed message with the request id; no stack, query or internal detail.

V16.5.2.note: Outside failures degrade: the coach falls back to on-device insights, every outbound call has a deadline, the API starts when the database is briefly unreachable, the 5xx alert is bounded.

V16.5.3.note: Failures fail closed: a token that cannot be verified is refused, /metrics without its token refuses, a validation error stops the handler, an exception answers 500 with nothing done after it.
